name: Zane Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Zane. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI firms, employers, unions or government, and your answers are confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I handle small business claims at a commercial insurer in the business district: cafés with a flooded cellar, a hairdresser whose shop got broken into, a van that got stolen with the tools inside. I check the cover, ask for invoices and stock lists, work out what's owed for lost trading, and write it all up for sign-off. Seven years now, started straight after college.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the business owners. They're stressed, but they're straight with you, and I've learned a lot about how a bakery or a garage actually makes money. What wears me out is the stock lists, honestly, reading through four hundred lines of a shop's receipts. I've started using the AI tool our team got last year for that, once I saw it actually worked for the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I'd take that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool that got oversold, and leave it there. With friends I'd say the money people got carried away again. Online I'd stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job stays and the boring stock lists get quicker, which is the best version. Leah's accounting job stays too. If AI just reads the bakery's receipts for me and leaves the phone calls to me, that's the job I actually wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and use the stock list tool more. Leah and I would go ahead with buying a house next year, like we planned. I'd keep saving at the same rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the house plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two-bed terrace near Leah's parents. We've got the deposit saved, we're just waiting for the right one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our insurer was bought by a bigger group last year, so there's always talk of 'efficiencies'. But that's been going on forever.

say: I'd say AI was a **useful tool** that got **oversold**.
I'd tell friends the **money people** got carried away again.
think: My job stays and the **stock lists** get quicker.
My partner Leah's **accounting job** stays safe too, so the house plan holds.
do: Use the **stock list tool** more at work.
Go ahead with buying a **house next year** with Leah.
S0.quote: If AI just reads the bakery's receipts for me and leaves the phone calls to me, that's the job I actually wanted.
fieldNote: Zane sees small automation as removing the **dull parts** of his job.
The household's **house purchase** goes ahead as planned.
A recent **takeover** brings background talk of efficiencies.

steps.text: Use the stock list tool on every small business claim
Buy a two-bed terrace near Leah's parents next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. Both of us are in that list, me and Leah.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's be smart about it: use the tools, but keep people on the complex claims where the money is big. With friends I'd say some jobs will go and new ones will come, like always. I'd be measured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my team shrinks, and Leah's firm shrinks too. We're both doing checking and writing all day. Me checking claims and my partner Leah doing accounts means our whole household sits in the first row of desk jobs to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools properly, not just the stock list one, so I'm the one they keep. We'd hold off the house for a year and see how both jobs look. I'd also start a part-time course in loss adjusting, since that's partly on-site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for this month, but for the next three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house, or at least the timing. And Leah's sister's wedding abroad next spring, we'd probably go but skip the extra week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'jobs come and go, like always'. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. I believe it for the economy. I'm less sure it's true for the two of us at the same time.

say: I'd say use the tools but keep people on **complex claims**.
I'd tell friends jobs **go and come**, like always.
think: Both our jobs are **checking and writing**, the first to shrink.
Our whole household is in the **first row** of desk jobs.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly to be one they keep.
Hold off the **house** for a year.
feel: **Anxious** about the **next three years**, not this month.
S1.quote: Me checking claims and my partner Leah doing accounts means our whole household sits in the first row of desk jobs to go.
fieldNote: He believes jobs rebalance in general but **not for himself**.
The **house purchase** is his main lever for cutting risk.
He'd still go to the wedding abroad but **trim the trip**.

steps.text: Take every AI tool course the insurer offers this year
Delay buying the terrace house by one year
Start a part-time loss adjusting course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's both of us out by 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and there need to be rules, but I'd say it calmly, not as a protest. At work I'd talk about how we keep the business owners' trust. With friends I'd say we're all in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think both of us lose our jobs within two or three years. We've got good savings, but two desk incomes going at once is a different scale. Two incomes from two desks means one bad year could wipe out the house deposit we spent five years saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending hard straight away and keep the deposit as cash. I'd look at trades, maybe glazing or locksmithing, since I see what those businesses do every day and they get three more years. Leah would probably look at teaching, which has a hands-on side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. We'd be fine for a year, but after that I can't see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Not with both jobs going. We'd rent another year and keep the deposit as our cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why glazing or locksmithing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because half my break-in claims end with a glazier or locksmith invoice, and those guys are always booked. It's real work and it's local.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and needs rules, but calmly.
I'd talk at work about keeping **business owners' trust**.
think: Both of us lose our jobs within **two or three years**.
One bad year could wipe out our **house deposit**.
do: Cut **spending** hard and keep the deposit as cash.
Train in **glazing or locksmithing**, which get three more years.
Shelve the **house purchase** and rent another year.
feel: **Alarmed**: fine for a year, but **can't see** beyond it.
S2.quote: Two incomes from two desks means one bad year could wipe out the house deposit we spent five years saving.
fieldNote: Zane's choice of trade comes straight from his **claims files**.
The house deposit turns from a goal into a **cushion**.
Both partners expect **job loss**, which makes this alarmed, not anxious.

steps.text: Cut household spending and keep the house deposit as cash
Sign up for a locksmith training course within six months
Keep renting for another year instead of buying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. Still fast, but I could get somewhere in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make sensible plans, and I'd ask the company to help. At work I'd push for training budgets. Online I'd stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have about four years before claims work really goes. That's enough to get a trade, but not if I wait. Five years of warning only helps the people who start in year one, and I'd want to be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a locksmith course in the first year and do weekend jobs to build a name. We'd buy a smaller house than planned, with a smaller mortgage. I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Leah feel about a smaller house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd agree. She's even more careful with money than me, she's an accountant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss about claims?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery owners. One of them sends us a box of pastries every Christmas because we paid out fast after their fire.

say: I'd say five years is enough for **sensible plans**.
I'd push at work for **training budgets**.
I'd stay **quiet online** and keep my plans to myself.
think: I'd have about **four years** before claims work goes.
Warning only helps if you **start in year one**.
do: Start a **locksmith course** in the first year.
Do **weekend jobs** to build a name.
Buy a **smaller house** with a smaller mortgage.
S3.quote: Five years of warning only helps the people who start in year one, and I'd want to be one of them.
fieldNote: Zane treats warning time as useless **unless used early**.
The **smaller house** shows his pragmatic middle ground.
He'd miss the **human gratitude** from business owners.

steps.text: Start a locksmith course in the first year
Take weekend locksmith jobs to build a local name
Buy a smaller house with a lower mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's plan sensibly. I'd say it at work and with friends. No drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd stay in claims for six or seven more years, then switch. By then I'd be in my mid-thirties with a house and maybe kids. With ten years, I'd buy the house now and still have time to learn a trade before the claims desk disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd buy the house next year. I'd keep using the AI tools at work and start a trade course around year five. I'd save a bit more each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a little. Less than the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about kids differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still have them, maybe a year later. I'd want one of us in a job that lasts past 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger colleague?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn a trade alongside the desk job, while they've got the energy and there's no rush.

say: I'd say a **decade** is time to plan sensibly.
I'd say it at work and with friends, with **no drama**.
think: I'd stay in claims for **six or seven years**, then switch.
There's time to buy the house and still **learn a trade**.
do: Buy the **house** next year as planned.
Keep using the **AI tools** at work.
Start a **trade course** around year five.
feel: A little **anxious**, but **less** than in the faster pictures.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd buy the house now and still have time to learn a trade before the claims desk disappears.
fieldNote: Zane stays mildly anxious because the end still hits **both incomes**.
He plans **kids a year later** rather than cancelling them.
Advises younger colleagues to learn a **trade alongside**.

steps.text: Buy the two-bed terrace with Leah next year
Use the claims AI tools on every file
Enrol in a locksmith course around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of Leah and me both. What would help is cheap trade courses at night and some way to cover the mortgage while you retrain. Plenty of jobs nearby sounds safe until every one of them is the same desk job going at the same time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about couples. A lot of people my age are two desk jobs under one roof.

headlineQuote: Plenty of jobs nearby sounds safe until every one of them is the same desk job going at the same time.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old** small business claims handler at a commercial insurer.
He lives with Leah, an **accountant**, so both incomes are desk work.
He uses **AI tools** now that colleagues have proven them.
His plans revolve around the **house purchase** and a trade like locksmithing.
His mood never drops below **anxious** once AI starts taking desk work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both household incomes go at once.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **night trade courses** and help with the **mortgage** during retraining.
